title: When to Retrain after Drift: CALIPER Test
one_liner: A test that watches how accurately a model can predict the next data point at different neighborhood sizes to decide if you have gathered enough new data to safely retrain after a sudden shift.
lead: When data suddenly changes, a trained model becomes unreliable. The practical question is: how much new data do you need to collect before retraining? CALIPER answers this without retraining—by running a lightweight test on the new data to measure whether patterns are stable enough to learn from.

paras: In streaming data, sudden concept drift—when the underlying pattern suddenly changes—breaks predictions. A model trained on old data can no longer guess the next value accurately.

A naive approach: collect some new data and retrain. But how much? Collect 10 samples? 100? Too little and the new model still overfits to noise; too much and you waste time waiting. There is no signal from the data itself saying 'now you have enough.'

callout.html: Dynamical systems have state dependence: nearby data points tend to stay nearby over time. Use that pattern to estimate data sufficiency without retraining.

steps.text: An external alarm signals the data pattern changed.
Gather new samples after the change. CALIPER runs on these.
Choose a single sample from the new data to predict.
For each neighborhood size, use the new data to predict that point.
If error keeps shrinking smoothly as neighborhoods grow, declare data sufficient.

paras: CALIPER replaces the manual 'guess and retrain' loop with an automated, data-only sufficiency test. It does not retrain; it only probes.

hidden.name: state dependence
paras: State dependence is a single number measuring whether neighbors stay neighbors over time. In a dynamical system, if you pick a data point and look at its neighbors right now, do they stay close to it one step into the future? If yes, the data has high state dependence. If neighbors scatter away, state dependence is low.

CALIPER estimates state dependence by fitting a model to neighboring points and measuring one-step prediction error. A smooth drop in error as the neighborhood grows signals stable neighborhoods, meaning the data pattern is learnable and retraining will generalize well.

heat.caption: Darker means lower one-step prediction error at larger neighborhoods. Monotone drop signals learnable patterns.

reads.html: If your new data points cluster stably in neighborhoods, retraining will work.
Monotone non-increasing trend in one-step proxy error under an effective sample size threshold indicates state dependence sufficient for safe retraining.

mechanism.h2: Why Monotone Error Drop Predicts Retraining Success
paras: When you collect new data after a drift, that data comes from a new dynamical system. The question is: does the new system have learnable patterns? CALIPER answers by testing neighborhoods.

Here is the mechanism: For a test point, fit a local model using only its nearest neighbors (tight neighborhood). Measure one-step prediction error. Now expand the neighborhood. Fit again. Measure again. If error keeps dropping smoothly as you expand, it means neighbors were genuinely informative—they were close to the point for a reason, not by accident. The farther points you add contribute real signal, not noise. This smoothly dropping error is a signature of a learnable pattern. When you retrain the real model on this data, it will generalize, because the data itself exhibits stable, repeatable structure.
If error jumps around or rises, neighborhoods are not stable. Adding more distant points makes the fit worse, signaling the data is too noisy or unstructured. Retraining on such data would fail.

stages.s: Fit local model at small neighborhood size
Expand neighborhood; fit and measure again

math.words: For each neighborhood size (locality parameter theta), solve weighted normal equations to fit a local model on neighbors, predict the test point, measure the absolute error. Check that error is non-increasing as theta grows.
symbols: the test point you want to predict
the model's prediction using neighborhood size theta
one-step prediction error at time t and neighborhood size theta

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Neighborhood tiny (theta=0.1): neighbors within 0.1 units. Fit 2 points. Predict y. Error = 0.8.
Neighborhood medium (theta=0.5): neighbors within 0.5 units. Fit 6 points. Predict y. Error = 0.5.
Neighborhood large (theta=1.0): neighbors within 1.0 units. Fit 15 points. Predict y. Error = 0.3.
Trend: 0.8 → 0.5 → 0.3 (monotone down). More data per fit means smoother model, better prediction. Sign of stable neighborhoods.

math.note: Monotone non-increasing error as neighborhoods grow is a proxy for state dependence—the deeper reason retraining will work.

items.html: If error jumps up and down, neighborhoods are unstable—nearby points are not genuinely related to each other. Distant points mislead more than they help because they add noise, not signal, so the fit gets worse as neighborhoods grow. Retraining on such noisy, incoherent data will fail. CALIPER correctly rejects this data size.
If post-drift data is sparse, neighborhoods are empty. No local model can be fit. CALIPER has an effective sample size gate to catch this.
If the new pattern changes again during collection, neighborhoods from early in the window no longer match later points. Monotonicity breaks. Correctly signals retraining is not ready.
CALIPER works because it tests a direct proxy for the property that makes retraining succeed: stable, learnable neighborhoods in the new data.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic streaming scenario with sudden drift. Generate two dynamical systems: before and after the drift. After drift detection, run CALIPER on the new data stream at different collection sizes. Plot CALIPER's decision (yes / no retrain ready) against the actual post-drift model's generalization error when retrained at that size. Show that CALIPER's 'yes' decisions align with low generalization error, and 'no' decisions align with high error. Use a simple learner (linear regression or nearest neighbor) to keep retraining fast.
demo.metric_eq: alignment = fraction of CALIPER decisions that match the true best retraining data size
demo.closing: The demo must show CALIPER avoids both the overfitting (retrain too early) and the delay (wait too long) traps.
